<div class="intro-box">
These problems review the central ideas from Chapter $18$. The questions increase gradually in difficulty from Question $1$ to Question $15$. Show the main mathematical steps, assess the relevant conditions and explain conclusions in context. Selected solutions include short R commands for verification. Unless stated otherwise, round probabilities to four decimal places and other numerical answers to at least three decimal places.
</div>

::: {.question-card}
### Question $1$

For each study, decide whether the data form two independent samples or matched pairs. State the appropriate procedure.

1. Recovery times are compared for unrelated dogs randomly assigned to two anaesthetic drugs.
2. Heart rate is measured before and after exercise in the same horses.
3. Shell thickness is compared for separate random samples of mussels from two bays.
4. Two blood analyzers test aliquots from each of the same patient specimens.
5. Growth is compared between unrelated seedlings randomly assigned to fertilizer and control groups.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The groups contain unrelated dogs, so use a Welch two-sample $t$ procedure.</li>
  <li>The two observations come from the same horse, so calculate within-horse differences and use a matched pairs $t$ procedure.</li>
  <li>The mussels in the two samples are unrelated, so use a Welch two-sample $t$ procedure.</li>
  <li>The measurements are paired within specimens. Analyze the instrument differences using a matched pairs $t$ procedure.</li>
  <li>The groups contain unrelated experimental units, so use a Welch two-sample $t$ procedure.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $2$

A veterinary trial compares population mean recovery time for a new analgesic and a standard analgesic. Let Group $1$ be the new treatment and Group $2$ be the standard treatment.

1. Define $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$.
2. State the parameter that measures the treatment difference.
3. If $\bar{x}_1=41.2$ minutes and $\bar{x}_2=47.5$ minutes, calculate the point estimate.
4. Interpret the sign of the estimate.
5. Explain what changes if the group labels are reversed.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>$\mu_1$ is the population mean recovery time under the new analgesic, and $\mu_2$ is the population mean recovery time under the standard analgesic.</li>
  <li>The parameter is $\mu_1-\mu_2$, defined as new minus standard.</li>
  <li>
  $$\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=41.2-47.5=\boxed{-6.3\text{ minutes}}$$
  </li>
  <li>The negative estimate means that the new-treatment sample mean is $6.3$ minutes lower than the standard-treatment sample mean.</li>
  <li>Reversing the labels changes the estimate to $+6.3$ minutes and reverses the sign of a confidence interval and test statistic. The magnitude and the two-sided $P$-value do not change.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $3$

A fish nutrition experiment independently assigns juvenile Atlantic salmon to two feeds.

| Feed | $n$ | Mean growth (g) | Standard deviation (g) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Feed A | $25$ | $82.4$ | $12.5$ |
| Feed B | $30$ | $76.1$ | $10.8$ |

Define the difference as Feed A minus Feed B.

1. Calculate the estimated difference in population means.
2. Calculate the contribution $s_1^2/n_1$ from Feed A.
3. Calculate the contribution $s_2^2/n_2$ from Feed B.
4. Calculate the Welch standard error.
5. Explain why the two variances are added even though the means are subtracted.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$82.4-76.1=\boxed{6.300\text{ g}}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}=\frac{12.5^2}{25}=\frac{156.25}{25}=\boxed{6.250}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}=\frac{10.8^2}{30}=\frac{116.64}{30}=\boxed{3.888}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{6.250+3.888}=\sqrt{10.138}\approx\boxed{3.184\text{ g}}$$
  </li>
  <li>For independent random variables, variances add when variables are added or subtracted. Uncertainty from both independent sample means contributes to the uncertainty of their difference.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $4$

Continue with the salmon-feed summaries from Question $3$.

1. Calculate the Welch--Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
2. Test $H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0$ against $H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq0$.
3. Calculate the two-sided $P$-value.
4. State the conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
5. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval and explain its relationship to the test.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$
  df=
  \frac{(6.250+3.888)^2}
  {\dfrac{6.250^2}{24}+\dfrac{3.888^2}{29}}
  \approx\boxed{47.829}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$t=\frac{6.300}{3.184}\approx\boxed{1.979}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$P=2P(T_{47.829}\geq1.979)\approx\boxed{0.0536}$$
  </li>
  <li>Because $0.0536>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. The data do not provide statistically significant evidence at the $5\%$ level that the population mean growth differs between the feeds.</li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.011$,
  $$6.300\pm2.011(3.184)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(-0.102,\ 12.702)\text{ g}}$$
  Zero lies inside the interval, agreeing with failure to reject the two-sided null hypothesis.</li>
</ol>

```{r q4-salmon-welch-test, echo=TRUE}
se <- sqrt(12.5^2 / 25 + 10.8^2 / 30)

df <- (12.5^2 / 25 + 10.8^2 / 30)^2 /
  ((12.5^2 / 25)^2 / 24 +
   (10.8^2 / 30)^2 / 29)

t_value <- (82.4 - 76.1) / se
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df)

c(SE = se, df = df, t = t_value, P_value = p_value)
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $5$

A field biologist compares the daily foraging time of bees in two independently sampled habitats.

| Habitat | $n$ | Mean time (minutes) | Standard deviation (minutes) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Restored meadow | $20$ | $34.2$ | $6.5$ |
| Roadside verge | $18$ | $29.8$ | $5.2$ |

Define the difference as restored meadow minus roadside verge.

1. Calculate the point estimate and standard error.
2. Calculate the Welch degrees of freedom.
3. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval.
4. Interpret the interval.
5. Does the interval provide evidence of a population mean difference at the $5\%$ level?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=34.2-29.8=4.400\text{ minutes}$$
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{6.5^2}{20}+\frac{5.2^2}{18}}\approx\boxed{1.901\text{ minutes}}$$
  </li>
  <li>The Welch formula gives
  $$df\approx\boxed{35.543}$$
  </li>
  <li>For $df\approx35.543$, $t^*\approx2.029$. Thus,
  $$4.400\pm2.029(1.901)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(0.542,\ 8.258)\text{ minutes}}$$
  </li>
  <li>We are $95\%$ confident that the population mean daily foraging time in restored meadows is between approximately $0.542$ and $8.258$ minutes greater than in roadside verges for habitats represented by the sampling process.</li>
  <li>Yes. The interval contains only positive values and excludes zero, so the corresponding two-sided test rejects equality at $\alpha=0.05$.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $6$

A vaccine study compares antibody concentrations between independently randomized vaccine and control groups.

| Group | $n$ | Mean concentration | Standard deviation |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Vaccine | $28$ | $156$ | $38$ |
| Control | $24$ | $133$ | $35$ |

The research question specified in advance is whether the vaccine increases the population mean antibody concentration.

1. State the hypotheses.
2. Calculate the standard error and Welch degrees of freedom.
3. Calculate the test statistic.
4. Calculate the one-sided $P$-value and state the conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
5. Can the difference be interpreted causally? Explain.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$H_0:\mu_V-\mu_C=0\qquad H_a:\mu_V-\mu_C>0$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{38^2}{28}+\frac{35^2}{24}}\approx\boxed{10.130}$$
  and the Welch formula gives
  $$df\approx\boxed{49.720}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$t=\frac{156-133}{10.130}\approx\boxed{2.271}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$P=P(T_{49.720}\geq2.271)\approx\boxed{0.0138}$$
  Because $0.0138<0.05$, reject $H_0$. The data provide statistically significant evidence that the vaccine increases the population mean antibody concentration.</li>
  <li>Yes, subject to proper implementation and other study limitations. Random assignment balances known and unknown confounding variables on average, supporting a causal comparison between the assigned treatments.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $7$

A veterinary hospital compares recovery time for unrelated animals receiving a new and standard treatment.

| Treatment | $n$ | Mean recovery (hours) | Standard deviation (hours) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| New | $22$ | $41.5$ | $8.2$ |
| Standard | $20$ | $47.8$ | $9.1$ |

The alternative specified before the study is that the new treatment reduces population mean recovery time.

1. State the hypotheses using new minus standard.
2. Calculate the standard error, degrees of freedom and test statistic.
3. Calculate the lower-tail $P$-value.
4. State the conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
5. Construct a two-sided $95\%$ confidence interval and interpret it.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$H_0:\mu_N-\mu_S=0\qquad H_a:\mu_N-\mu_S<0$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{8.2^2}{22}+\frac{9.1^2}{20}}\approx\boxed{2.683}$$
  $$df\approx\boxed{38.448}$$
  $$t=\frac{41.5-47.8}{2.683}\approx\boxed{-2.348}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$P=P(T_{38.448}\leq-2.348)\approx\boxed{0.0120}$$
  </li>
  <li>Reject $H_0$. The data provide statistically significant evidence that the new treatment reduces population mean recovery time.</li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.024$,
  $$-6.300\pm2.024(2.683)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(-11.729,\ -0.871)\text{ hours}}$$
  We are $95\%$ confident that the new treatment reduces population mean recovery time by approximately $0.871$ to $11.729$ hours.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $8$

A veterinary study compares blood lactate concentrations after two independent fluid-therapy protocols.

| Protocol | $n$ | Mean lactate (mmol/L) | Standard deviation |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| A | $16$ | $2.4$ | $0.7$ |
| B | $18$ | $2.8$ | $0.9$ |

1. State hypotheses for a two-sided comparison.
2. Calculate the standard error and test statistic.
3. Calculate the Welch degrees of freedom and $P$-value.
4. State the conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
5. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval and explain why a large $P$-value does not prove equality.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq0$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{0.7^2}{16}+\frac{0.9^2}{18}}=\boxed{0.275}$$
  $$t=\frac{2.4-2.8}{0.275}\approx\boxed{-1.455}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$df\approx\boxed{31.485}$$
  $$P=2P(T_{31.485}\geq1.455)\approx\boxed{0.1557}$$
  </li>
  <li>Because $0.1557>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. The data do not provide statistically significant evidence of a difference in population mean lactate concentration.</li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.038$,
  $$-0.400\pm2.038(0.275)=\boxed{(-0.961,\ 0.161)\text{ mmol/L}}$$
  The interval contains negative values, zero and positive values. The data are compatible with several population differences; they do not establish that the means are exactly equal.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $9$

An insurance analyst compares claim amounts for two independently sampled policy groups.

| Policy group | $n$ | Mean claim | Standard deviation |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Group $1$ | $60$ | $\$1450$ | $\$400$ |
| Group $2$ | $55$ | $\$1320$ | $\$350$ |

1. Calculate the point estimate and standard error.
2. Calculate the Welch degrees of freedom and two-sided test statistic.
3. Calculate the two-sided $P$-value.
4. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval.
5. Explain how the interval and test agree, and comment on practical importance.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=1450-1320=\$130$$
  $$\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{400^2}{60}+\frac{350^2}{55}}\approx\boxed{\$69.957}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$df\approx\boxed{112.766}$$
  $$t=\frac{130}{69.957}\approx\boxed{1.858}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$P\approx\boxed{0.0657}$$
  </li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx1.981$,
  $$130\pm1.981(69.957)=\boxed{(-\$8.600,\ \$268.600)}$$
  </li>
  <li>The interval includes zero, so the corresponding two-sided test fails to reject at $\alpha=0.05$. Nevertheless, differences as large as approximately $\$269$ remain compatible with the data. Whether such a difference is financially important should be evaluated separately from statistical significance.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $10$

Researchers compare mean body mass for urban and rural songbirds. They capture birds at one easily accessible urban park and one easily accessible rural reserve. The urban sample mean is lower, and a Welch test gives $P=0.002$.

1. Is this a randomized experiment or an observational study?
2. Does the small $P$-value establish that urban habitat causes lower body mass?
3. Identify two plausible confounding variables.
4. Explain the population to which the result can reasonably generalize.
5. Suggest one design improvement.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>This is an observational study because habitat was not randomly assigned.</li>
  <li>No. The small $P$-value is evidence of an association between site and body mass under the statistical model. It does not remove confounding or selection bias.</li>
  <li>Plausible confounders include species composition, bird age, sex, food availability, disease prevalence, migration stage and time of capture.</li>
  <li>Because only one convenient site of each type was used, generalization should be limited to birds similar to those captured at those sites and times. The two sites do not represent all urban and rural habitats.</li>
  <li>The researchers could randomly sample several urban and rural sites, use the same capture protocol and season at every site, and record important biological covariates. Replication at the habitat level is especially important.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $11$

An R data frame contains a quantitative variable `growth` and a factor `diet` with levels `"Control"` and `"Supplement"`. The goal is to estimate

$$
\mu_{\text{Supplement}}-\mu_{\text{Control}}
$$

1. Write an R command that performs a Welch two-sample $t$ test.
2. Explain why the factor-level order must be checked.
3. If R reports Control minus Supplement, how should the estimate and confidence interval be converted to Supplement minus Control?
4. Which argument requests a one-sided alternative that Supplement is greater?
5. Why should `var.equal = TRUE` generally not be added?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>First make Supplement the reference, or first, factor level, and then run the Welch test:
  ```{r q11-welch-command, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
study_data$diet <- relevel(
  study_data$diet,
  ref = "Supplement"
)

t.test(growth ~ diet, data = study_data)
  ```
  R uses Welch's method by default.</li>
  <li>The factor-level order determines which mean is subtracted from which. The sign of the estimate, test statistic and interval depends on this order.</li>
  <li>If the reported estimate is Control minus Supplement, multiply the estimate by $-1$. For an interval $(L,U)$, the reversed interval is $(-U,-L)$.</li>
  <li>After ensuring that Supplement is the first group in the comparison, use
  ```{r q11-one-sided-command, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
t.test(
  growth ~ diet,
  data = study_data,
  alternative = "greater"
)
  ```
  </li>
  <li>Setting `var.equal = TRUE` requests the pooled procedure, which assumes equal population variances. Welch's method does not require this assumption and is reliable whether the variances are equal or unequal.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $12$

Two independent samples have the following summaries:

| Group | $n$ | $\bar{x}$ | $s$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| $1$ | $10$ | $100$ | $20$ |
| $2$ | $40$ | $94$ | $5$ |

1. Calculate the Welch standard error.
2. Calculate the Welch test statistic for equal population means.
3. Calculate the pooled variance and pooled standard error.
4. Calculate the pooled test statistic.
5. Explain why the pooled analysis is risky in this example.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}_{W}
  =\sqrt{\frac{20^2}{10}+\frac{5^2}{40}}
  =\sqrt{40+0.625}
  \approx\boxed{6.374}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$t_W=\frac{100-94}{6.374}\approx\boxed{0.941}$$
  The Welch degrees of freedom are approximately $9.283$.</li>
  <li>
  $$s_p^2=
  \frac{(10-1)20^2+(40-1)5^2}{10+40-2}
  =\frac{3600+975}{48}
  =\boxed{95.313}
  $$
  Therefore,
  $$s_p=\sqrt{95.313}\approx9.763$$
  and
  $$\operatorname{SE}_p
  =9.763\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{40}}
  \approx\boxed{3.452}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$t_p=\frac{100-94}{3.452}\approx\boxed{1.738}$$
  </li>
  <li>The smaller group has much greater variability. Pooling spreads the large variance across all $50$ observations and produces an unrealistically small standard error for the difference. The unequal variances are paired with strongly unequal sample sizes, precisely the setting in which the pooled method can be misleading. Welch's method should be used.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $13$

A veterinary clinic records recovery time, in minutes, for unrelated animals receiving a new or standard anaesthetic protocol.

| New protocol | Standard protocol |
|--:|--:|
| $36$ | $48$ |
| $42$ | $44$ |
| $39$ | $46$ |
| $45$ | $50$ |
| $40$ | $43$ |
| $38$ | $47$ |
| $41$ | $45$ |
| $37$ | $49$ |
|  | $42$ |

The alternative specified in advance is that the new protocol reduces population mean recovery time.

1. Calculate the sample means and sample standard deviations.
2. Calculate the Welch standard error and degrees of freedom.
3. Calculate the test statistic and lower-tail $P$-value.
4. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval.
5. State the conclusion and identify the design feature needed for a causal interpretation.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>For the new protocol,
  $$n_1=8,\qquad \bar{x}_1=39.750,\qquad s_1\approx2.915$$
  For the standard protocol,
  $$n_2=9,\qquad \bar{x}_2=46.000,\qquad s_2\approx2.739$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}
  =\sqrt{\frac{2.915^2}{8}+\frac{2.739^2}{9}}
  \approx\boxed{1.377}
  $$
  and
  $$df\approx\boxed{14.488}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$t=\frac{39.750-46.000}{1.377}\approx\boxed{-4.539}$$
  $$P=P(T_{14.488}\leq-4.539)\approx\boxed{0.0002}$$
  </li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.138$,
  $$-6.250\pm2.138(1.377)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(-9.194,\ -3.306)\text{ minutes}}$$
  </li>
  <li>The data provide very strong evidence that the new protocol reduces population mean recovery time. A causal interpretation requires random assignment of animals to the two protocols, along with comparable treatment and measurement procedures.</li>
</ol>

```{r q13-anaesthetic-test, echo=TRUE}
new_protocol <- c(36, 42, 39, 45, 40, 38, 41, 37)
standard_protocol <- c(48, 44, 46, 50, 43, 47, 45, 49, 42)

t.test(
  new_protocol,
  standard_protocol,
  alternative = "less",
  var.equal = FALSE
)
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $14$

Marine biologists independently sample adult sea turtles from coastal and offshore feeding areas. Mean sustained swimming speeds are summarized below.

| Area | $n$ | Mean speed (m/s) | Standard deviation (m/s) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coastal | $18$ | $2.84$ | $0.36$ |
| Offshore | $16$ | $2.61$ | $0.41$ |

1. Calculate the estimated coastal-minus-offshore difference.
2. Calculate the standard error, degrees of freedom and test statistic.
3. Calculate the two-sided $P$-value.
4. Construct and interpret a $95\%$ confidence interval.
5. Explain why the absence of statistical significance does not imply equal swimming speeds.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$2.84-2.61=\boxed{0.230\text{ m/s}}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$\operatorname{SE}
  =\sqrt{\frac{0.36^2}{18}+\frac{0.41^2}{16}}
  \approx\boxed{0.133\text{ m/s}}
  $$
  $$df\approx\boxed{30.122}$$
  $$t=\frac{0.230}{0.133}\approx\boxed{1.728}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$P\approx\boxed{0.0941}$$
  </li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.042$,
  $$0.230\pm2.042(0.133)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(-0.042,\ 0.502)\text{ m/s}}$$
  We are $95\%$ confident that the coastal population mean is between approximately $0.042$ m/s lower and $0.502$ m/s higher than the offshore population mean.</li>
  <li>The interval contains a range of negative and positive differences in addition to zero. The study lacks sufficient precision to determine the direction at the $5\%$ level; it does not establish that the means are identical.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $15$

A randomized veterinary experiment assigns $24$ animals independently to a new or standard analgesic. Recovery times, in minutes, are

| New analgesic | Standard analgesic |
|--:|--:|
| $42$ | $49$ |
| $38$ | $46$ |
| $45$ | $52$ |
| $40$ | $48$ |
| $36$ | $44$ |
| $44$ | $50$ |
| $39$ | $47$ |
| $41$ | $53$ |
| $37$ | $45$ |
| $43$ | $51$ |
| $40$ | $48$ |
| $39$ | $46$ |

1. Describe the study design and state the hypotheses for testing whether the new analgesic reduces population mean recovery time.
2. Calculate the sample summaries, point estimate and standard error.
3. Calculate the Welch degrees of freedom, test statistic and one-sided $P$-value.
4. Construct and interpret a two-sided $95\%$ confidence interval.
5. State the scientific conclusion, explain what random assignment contributes and verify the result using R.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>This is a randomized comparative experiment with two independent treatment groups. Define the difference as new minus standard:
  $$H_0:\mu_N-\mu_S=0\qquad H_a:\mu_N-\mu_S<0$$
  </li>
  <li>For the new analgesic,
  $$n_1=12,\qquad \bar{x}_1=40.333,\qquad s_1\approx2.774$$
  For the standard analgesic,
  $$n_2=12,\qquad \bar{x}_2=48.250,\qquad s_2\approx2.832$$
  The point estimate is
  $$40.333-48.250=\boxed{-7.917\text{ minutes}}$$
  and
  $$\operatorname{SE}
  =\sqrt{\frac{2.774^2}{12}+\frac{2.832^2}{12}}
  \approx\boxed{1.145\text{ minutes}}
  $$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$df\approx\boxed{21.991}$$
  $$t=\frac{-7.917}{1.145}\approx\boxed{-6.917}$$
  $$P=P(T_{21.991}\leq-6.917)\approx\boxed{0.0000003}$$
  </li>
  <li>Using $t^*\approx2.074$,
  $$-7.917\pm2.074(1.145)$$
  gives
  $$\boxed{(-10.290,\ -5.543)\text{ minutes}}$$
  We are $95\%$ confident that the new analgesic reduces the population mean recovery time by approximately $5.543$ to $10.290$ minutes relative to the standard analgesic.</li>
  <li>The data provide extremely strong evidence that the new analgesic reduces mean recovery time. Random assignment supports a causal treatment comparison by balancing potential confounding variables on average. Generalization beyond animals like those studied still depends on how the animals were selected.</li>
</ol>

```{r q15-analgesic-welch-test, echo=TRUE}
new_analgesic <- c(
  42, 38, 45, 40, 36, 44,
  39, 41, 37, 43, 40, 39
)

standard_analgesic <- c(
  49, 46, 52, 48, 44, 50,
  47, 53, 45, 51, 48, 46
)

t.test(
  new_analgesic,
  standard_analgesic,
  alternative = "less",
  var.equal = FALSE
)
```
</div>
</details>
:::
